stem:
Harry, a 2-year-old boy, presents with a barking cough and stridor at rest. He had been well until this evening apart from a mild runny nose and slight cough. On examination he has moderate respiratory distress with intercostal and subcostal recessions and tug. His RR is 35, HR 140 and saturations 94% in room air. He has a clear chest and inspiratory stridor at rest. He has been previously well and his immunisations are up to date.

He is given oxygen via a face mask, nebulised adrenaline, and dexamethasone. He has minimal response and requires a further dose of nebulised adrenaline.

On review he is febrile to 39°C, appears flushed and unwell, prefers to lie flat, and has a respiratory rate of 45 with a HR of 160. His stridor is now soft and biphasic.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bacterial tracheitis is the best diagnosis. A child with an initial croup-like presentation who becomes febrile, toxic-appearing, and responds poorly to nebulised adrenaline should raise concern for bacterial tracheitis. Biphasic stridor and worsening distress also support upper airway infection beyond uncomplicated croup.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Breathing difficulties

rationale: The question already had suitable options; the best existing option was selected.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: severe upper airway infection with fever, toxic appearance, poor response to adrenaline, and biphasic stridor is typical of bacterial tracheitis.
optionExplanations.B: A foreign body usually has a more abrupt onset and does not typically cause fever and toxic appearance like this.
optionExplanations.C: Epiglottitis can cause drooling, muffled voice, and tripod positioning, but the preceding barking cough and poor response pattern here fit bacterial tracheitis better.
optionExplanations.D: Simple croup usually improves with adrenaline and dexamethasone and is less likely to cause marked fever and toxic appearance.
optionExplanations.E: Diphtheria is uncommon in immunised children and would more typically cause a pharyngeal pseudomembrane and systemic toxicity.
